summary:
Lunar Maps is a browser tool that integrates a wide range of lunar data to provide detailed analysis of the site performance, while allowing users to quickly compare sites . For any site and time window, it shows where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the real terrain horizon, and from that when a lander has sunlight, when Earth is visible, and when a Deep Space Network station can be reached.

It offers preset sites of existing and past missions, plus the ability to choose custom coordinates. Views include a sky panorama, engineering data graphs, a 2D map, a 3D Moon with time-driven shadows, and a first-person lander view. Planners can model solar array layouts and battery life, compare up to four scenarios side by side, search for the best start date, and export results.

Custom site selector enables evaluations and comparisons on-the-fly, and even evaluate design modification of solar array, accelerating selection of viable alternatives. Lunar Maps is a one-stop-shop with a simple interface that offers the detailed analysis of existing tools, while being easy enough for even non-specialists to use. Multiple visualization methods allow for intuitive understanding and aids in communicating ideas that raw data cannot.
details:
Lunar Maps is an interactive mission-planning prototype that helps users explore a critical question: where and when can a lunar lander receive sunlight, maintain power, and potentially communicate with Earth? Built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, it focuses on the Moon’s south pole, where the Sun and Earth appear close to the horizon and small terrain features can significantly affect a mission.
The app combines NASA LRO LOLA elevation data, LROC surface imagery, and NASA/JPL Horizons ephemerides. It models the surrounding terrain skyline and compares it with the positions of the Sun and Earth to estimate visibility over time. Users can explore 44 preset sites or enter custom coordinates, switch between 3D Moon, lander, sky, and 2D map views, and scrub through a mission timeline. Power and battery estimates connect this geometry to practical operating constraints.
Users can compare up to four scenarios by changing landing sites, arrival dates, mast heights, mission durations, and power assumptions. An arrival-window search ranks candidate dates and highlights battery constraints. Mission Copilot provides guided demonstrations and contextual explanations, while Guide and Expert modes accommodate different levels of experience. Scenario links and CSV exports make results easier to share and examine.
The project’s main benefit is making complex lunar data easier to understand and use together. A promising location may receive sunlight but lose sight of Earth; a later arrival may improve contact opportunities while introducing a longer battery deficit. Lunar Maps helps users see these trade-offs instead of relying on a single score. Its intended impact is to support early mission exploration, education, and informed discussion between people with different technical backgrounds. It is a prototype for exploratory analysis, rather than a flight-qualified planning system.
We developed the application using JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, with WebGL2 for interactive 3D visualization. Python, including NumPy, SciPy, and Pillow, supports terrain and imagery processing. Node.js supports local development and the optional AI backend, and the app is hosted on Vercel. Mission Copilot integrates OpenAI and Groq models for explanations; the browser’s simulation engine performs the calculations. We also used Remotion and ElevenLabs to produce a narrated demonstration video.
Lunar Maps is creative in how it connects a global view of the Moon with the perspective of a lander and the consequences for an entire mission. Users can move from seeing Earth near the terrain horizon to testing whether a taller mast changes visibility, then compare the resulting operating windows. This turns abstract datasets into an interactive explanation of cause and effect.
Our team considered terrain resolution, low-angle illumination, Earth visibility, potential Deep Space Network contact, battery capacity, solar-panel configuration, and arrival-date uncertainty. We also prioritized accessibility, browser performance, reproducible examples, and transparent assumptions. The app distinguishes potential line-of-sight contact from guaranteed communications and makes clear that factors such as station scheduling, radio performance, thermal survival, and battery aging require further mission-specific analysis
